summary.text: Galois theory, introduced by Évariste Galois, provides a connection between field theory and group theory.
Galois created it to study roots of polynomials, describing which equations can be solved by radicals through the permutation group of their roots.
It explains why equations of degree four or lower can be solved with roots and arithmetic, while most of degree five or higher cannot.

facts.label: Introduced by
facts.value: Évariste Galois, to study roots of polynomials

facts.label: Equations with formulas
facts.value: All of degree four or lower can be solved by radicals

items.prompt: A friend notes that quadratic, cubic and quartic equations all have root formulas, and assumes every higher-degree equation must too. What does Galois theory say?

options.label: Every equation has such a formula, though finding it gets harder with degree
Most equations of degree five or higher have no such formula
Formulas exist only for equations of even degree, such as six
Formulas exist for degree five but not for degree six or more

items.explain: Galois theory explains why equations of degree four or lower can be solved this way and why most of degree five or higher cannot.

items.prompt: Which description fits an equation that is solvable by radicals?

options.label: Its roots can be read off a graph where the curve crosses the axis
Every one of its roots turns out to be a whole number
Its roots can be written using only addition and subtraction
Its roots come from a formula using integers, nth roots and the four basic operations

items.explain: By definition, the roots must be expressible by a formula involving only integers, nth roots and the four basic arithmetic operations.

items.prompt: To decide whether an equation can be solved by radicals, Galois looked at a property of what?

options.label: The permutation group of the equation's roots
How large the roots are compared with the coefficients
How many of the roots are positive real numbers
Whether the roots add up to a whole number

items.explain: He characterized solvable equations in terms of properties of the permutation group of their roots.

items.prompt: The Abel–Ruffini theorem says a general polynomial of degree five or more cannot be solved by radicals. You hold one particular fifth-degree equation. What extra does Galois theory give you?

options.label: A promise that this equation is always solvable in the end
A numerical method to approximate its roots to any accuracy
A proof that its roots must all be real numbers
A clear test, even expressible as an algorithm, for whether this one equation is solvable

items.explain: Galois theory gives a conceptually clear means of determining whether a particular equation can be solved, one that can be written as an algorithm.

paragraphs.heading: What Galois theory is
paragraphs.text: Galois theory, begun by Évariste Galois, links two parts of algebra: the theory of fields and the theory of groups. The link, called the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, lets certain questions about fields be turned into questions about groups, which are simpler and easier to understand. The theory has since been generalized to Galois connections and to Grothendieck's Galois theory.

paragraphs.heading: The question behind it
paragraphs.text: Galois created the subject to study the roots of polynomials. An equation is called solvable by radicals if its roots can be written with a formula that uses only integers, nth roots and the four basic operations of arithmetic. Galois described which equations have this property in terms of the permutation group of their roots. This reaches far beyond the Abel–Ruffini theorem, which says a general polynomial of degree five or more cannot be solved by radicals.

paragraphs.heading: What it explains
paragraphs.text: The theory explains why some equations, including every equation of degree four or lower, can be solved this way, and why most equations of degree five or higher cannot. It also gives a way to decide whether a particular equation can be solved. That test is clear as an idea and can be written down as an algorithm.

paragraphs.heading: Before Galois
paragraphs.text: The cubic equation was first partly solved by Scipione del Ferro, who did not publish his method, and Niccolò Fontana Tartaglia found it again in 1535. Gerolamo Cardano extended it to many other cases and published it in his 1545 Ars Magna, which also held his student Lodovico Ferrari's solution of the quartic. In 1799 Paolo Ruffini almost proved that the quintic has no general solution by radicals, using permutation groups, and Niels Henrik Abel closed the gap with a proof in 1824.

paragraphs.heading: A rejected paper
paragraphs.text: In 1830, at 18, Galois sent a memoir on solvability by radicals to the French Academy of Sciences. It was rejected in 1831 as too sketchy and for stating its condition through the roots of the equation rather than its coefficients. Galois died in a duel in 1832, and Joseph Liouville published the paper in 1846, with some explanations of his own.

paragraphs.heading: Slow acceptance
paragraphs.text: Galois' contemporaries found the theory very hard to understand, let alone build on; even Liouville's 1846 commentary missed the group ideas at its heart. Joseph Alfred Serret put it in the 1866 edition of his algebra textbook, and his pupil Camille Jordan understood it better still in an 1870 book. Outside France it stayed obscure for longer, until Eugen Netto's books of the 1880s and Heinrich Martin Weber's 1895 textbook opened it to German and American readers.
